Dismantle
dis-MAN-tl
verb
From Old French desmanteler, to strip of a cloak or tear down the walls of a fortress (des-, away + manteler, to cloak). Literally to pull a structure to pieces. In recent activist usage it has become the verb of permanent revolution — to 'dismantle systems,' 'dismantle whiteness,' 'dismantle patriarchy,' 'dismantle the structures' — treating the existing order itself as the thing to be torn down.

⚖️ Biblical Verdict

🔴
Reject
The verb of permanent revolution turned against God's design; He builds and orders His house, and does not commission its demolition.

📖 Biblical Definition

Scripture knows a true tearing-down, but it is God's prerogative and always serves a building-up. 'A time to break down, and a time to build up' (Eccl. 3:3); the LORD set Jeremiah 'to root out, and to pull down... to build, and to plant' (Jer. 1:10) — the pulling-down ordered toward the planting. God Himself 'breaketh down, and it cannot be built again' (Job 12:14) where He judges; and Christ overthrew the moneychangers' tables in zeal for His Father's house (John 2:15). But the consistent biblical posture toward God's own ordained order — creation, the family, the church, the offices He appoints — is not demolition but reverence and right order: 'God is not the author of confusion, but of peace' (1 Cor. 14:33), and 'Let all things be done decently and in order' (1 Cor. 14:40). The Builder of the house (Heb. 3:4) does not commission His servants to tear down what He has built; He commissions them to build on the foundation already laid (1 Cor. 3:10-11).

📜 Origin & Era

An activist verb of permanent revolution ('dismantle systems / whiteness / patriarchy') importing endless tearing-down into the church; but God builds and orders His own design — 'decently and in order' (1 Cor. 14:33, 40) — He does not authorize its demolition.

DISMANTLE, verb. To strip of covering; to pull down or take to pieces, as the walls of a fortress.

From Old French desmanteler, to unclothe or raze.

Activist usage: the verb of permanent revolution — 'dismantle' systems, structures, whiteness, patriarchy — the standing order treated as the thing to be demolished.

Rebutted where it is turned against God's ordained order: He is 'not the author of confusion, but of peace' (1 Cor. 14:33) and commands all things 'decently and in order' (1 Cor. 14:40).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 14:33 — "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints."

1 Corinthians 14:40 — "Let all things be done decently and in order."

Ecclesiastes 3:3 — "A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;"

Jeremiah 1:10 — "See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant."

Hebrews 3:4 — "For every house is builded by some man; but he that built all things is God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

An ordinary verb is conscripted into permanent revolution — 'dismantle' the structures, the systems, the order — and carried into the church to set demolition against the very design God built; but the Builder's commission is to build on His foundation, not to raze it.

expand to see more

The corruption is a posture, not just a word. In activist usage 'dismantle' assumes that the existing order — of authority, of family, of sex, of inherited institutions — is fundamentally an apparatus of oppression, so that the faithful act is always to tear it down and the suspect act is to conserve, honor, or repair. Imported into the church, this reverses the biblical instinct entirely. Scripture's stance toward what God has ordained is reverence and order, not demolition; 'God is not the author of confusion, but of peace' (1 Cor. 14:33). The man whose first reflex toward headship, the offices of the church, or the creational order is to 'dismantle' it has adopted the spirit of the age, which mistakes God's architecture for a prison. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the activist sense of 'dismantle' is named here to rebut it.

Scripture does authorize a tearing-down — but observe its two strict limits. First, it is God's act and God's commission: He 'breaketh down' (Job 12:14), and He set Jeremiah to 'pull down' (Jer. 1:10); it is not a license seized by the discontented to raze whatever order displeases them. Second, every lawful pulling-down serves a building-up: Jeremiah is to pull down AND 'to build, and to plant'; Ecclesiastes pairs 'a time to break down' with 'a time to build up' (Eccl. 3:3). The activist 'dismantle' severs the demolition from any building — it is permanent revolution, tearing-down as a way of life, with no rest and no house at the end. That is not reformation; it is Babel in reverse.

The recovery is to remember Who builds. 'Every house is builded by some man; but he that built all things is God' (Heb. 3:4). The Reformation itself was not a dismantling of the church but a recovery of it — tearing down accumulated corruptions precisely in order to rebuild on the foundation already laid, 'which is Jesus Christ' (1 Cor. 3:11). The faithful do pull down idols, false teaching, and sin; but they do so as servants of the Builder, to clear the ground for His building, never to leave the soul or the church in rubble. Where God has built, our work is to build with Him — 'decently and in order' (1 Cor. 14:40).

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

An activist verb of permanent revolution turned against God's ordained order; Scripture allows a tearing-down only as God's act, always serving a building-up (Jer. 1:10; Eccl. 3:3). The Builder commissions us to build on His foundation, not to raze it.

Old French: desmanteler, to unclothe or raze a fortress — literally to pull a structure to pieces.

Activist sense: 'dismantle systems / whiteness / patriarchy' — permanent revolution, the standing order itself the target.

Biblical order: 1 Cor. 14:33, 40 — God is not the author of confusion but of peace; all things 'decently and in order.'

Usage

"They wanted to 'dismantle' the very order God built, mistaking His architecture for a prison and calling demolition reform."

"Jeremiah was sent to pull down AND to plant; the activist keeps the tearing-down and forgets there was ever to be a house."

"The Reformers did not raze the church; they cleared its corruptions to rebuild on the one foundation, Jesus Christ."
